### Why is this Important?

Stories are a memorable way to communicate that your organization values learning from mistakes. The goal is to create a habit of telling stories that encourage your team to find new and better ways of doing things, as well as to demonstrate important safety concerns, risks, or ways in which safety affects patients and healthcare workers at your organization. **Below are some suggestions to get started:**

- Tell real stories using real-life examples of past safety incidents or near-misses at your organization. Raising awareness regarding the risks, events, and opportunities for improvement through story-telling as it relates to safety is a powerful tool. 

- Write out a list of the 3-5 most useful examples of safety incidents or near misses from which practical lessons can be learned that you or your team have experienced over the past year. Pick the one that best reinforces the importance of attention to safety. Think about how you would convey this as a story for staff members:

>Who was involved?  
>When and where did it happen?  
>What was happening at the time?  
>What was the risk?  
>How was the incident resolved?  
>What did you learn from the incident or near miss?  
>How can safety issues like this be prevented in the future?  

- Take a few minutes in meetings and impromptu gatherings to share those stories to increase safety awareness and promote an understanding of the safety risks common at your organization. 

>Source: 

>The Joint Commission. Improving Patient and Worker Safety: Opportunities for Synergy, Collaboration and Innovation. Oakbrook Terrace, IL: The Joint Commission, Nov 2012. [http://www.jointcommission.org/](http://www.jointcommission.org/).
